prerequisites: Content covered in Calculus I and Physics I and II are extremely useful for understanding this course.

learning_outcomes.text: The graduate in Medical Engineering will be able to develop and understand electrical circuits and apply concepts related to Electrical Engineering.

The course provides new engineering knowledge, and the graduate will acquire understanding skills applicable to the comprehension, use, management, and maintenance of electrical or electronic machines, devices, and systems for biomedical applications.
The student will know and be able to understand the theoretical and practical foundations of Electromagnetism, Circuits, and Electrical Engineering.
The student will be able to comprehend the operation of electrical networks in steady-state, sinusoidal, and dynamic conditions.
The student will be able to analyze and synthesize simple electrical and electronic problems and devices.
They will be capable of designing basic electrical circuits in various operating regimes (steady-state, sinusoidal, and dynamic).
Moreover, they will be able to evaluate the most relevant measurement electrical signals.

The student will be able to independently develop design proposals and will acquire critical thinking and independent judgment regarding scientific issues in Electrical Engineering and Electromagnetism.

The student will be able to communicate solutions to scientific problems presented during the course and independently develop design proposals, innovative products, and compare different technologies, assessing their social, economic, and ethical implications.
The student will be able to clearly and accurately communicate information, problems, techniques, and solutions acquired during the course, both to specialists and non-specialists.
The student will develop methodological, applicative, and metacognitive skills that will enable continuous learning and updating throughout both their academic and professional careers.
Consequently, the graduate will possess a set of strategies aimed at enhancing their competences and skills, particularly those required to meet workplace demands (Lifelong Learning).

syllabus_topics: Circuit model: two-terminal elements, Kirchhoff’s laws
Active, passive, dissipative, and conservative components; linear and nonlinear, dynamic and non-dynamic, time-varying and time-invariant elements
Main two-terminal components: resistor, capacitor, inductor, switch, open circuit and short circuit, diodes, ideal and real voltage and current sources, controlled sources
Considerations on the characteristic of a two-terminal element and the maximum deliverable power
Introduction to the limitations of the circuit model
CIRCUIT PROPERTIES – ANALYSIS METHODS – DC CIRCUITS
Elements of graph theory: tree, co-tree, loop, ring, cut-set, incidence and fundamental loop matrices, Kirchhoff’s equations in matrix form, linearly independent Kirchhoff’s equations (proof)
Conservation of electrical power and Tellegen’s theorem (proof)
Concept of equivalent two-terminal element, resistors in series and parallel
Properties of linear resistive circuits, equivalent resistance, voltage and current dividers, superposition principle
Thevenin-Norton equivalent generators (proof) and their applications
Dynamics of first-order RC and RL circuits
Dynamics of second-order circuits: series RLC
Properties of state equations for RLC, RC, and RL second-order circuits
SINUSOIDAL STEADY-STATE CIRCUITS AND THREE-PHASE SYSTEMS
Sinusoidal steady-state circuits, phasors, phasor method (symbolic method), impedance, impedance circuit properties, reactance, admittance, susceptance
Circuit elements under sinusoidal steady-state conditions and phasor diagrams
Instantaneous and average power in sinusoidal regime; complex, active, reactive, apparent power and conservation properties
Advantages of three-phase over single-phase systems
Power supply of a balanced three-phase load
ANALYSIS AND SYNTHESIS OF TWO-PORT NETWORKS
Resistive two-port networks and matrix representations (G and R)
First, second, and third forms of reciprocity in resistive two-port networks (proofs)
Analysis and synthesis of two-port networks
Mutual coupling between inductors and equivalent circuits
teaching_methods: Lectures covering the theoretical and methodological topics of the course
Tutorials focused on solving exercises using the presented methods
Practice exercises with solutions, provided for self-assessment of individual preparation

assessment_methods.method: Written test (two mandatory exercises on dynamic circuits, sinusoidal steady-state circuits, and DC circuits; one or more optional exercises covering other topics)
Oral exam (two topics from the syllabus, explanations, proofs, examples)

assessment_rules: The written test is graded using symbolic marks from A (highest) to INS (insufficient). The written exam is considered sufficient if the two mandatory exercises are substantially solved without major conceptual errors. If the written exam is passed with a grade of D, the oral exam begins with an additional exercise. The final grade is Voto Finale, based on both components.
